learningObjective: Distinguish dynamic and static activation quantization by scale computation and runtime cost.

canonicalClaims.claim: Dynamic quantization computes activation scale/zero-point from the runtime tensor's statistics at each forward pass; static quantization computes and freezes them offline via a calibration pass over representative inputs.
conditions: The framework distinguishes these two modes (TensorRT, PyTorch, TF-Lite).
For static, a representative calibration set is available.
nonImplications: Does not imply dynamic is always slower — per-tensor reductions are cheap.
Does not imply static is always less accurate — frozen scales avoid drift from single-sample outliers.

misconceptions.claim: Dynamic quantization is a synonym for QAT and static quantization is a synonym for PTQ.
misconceptions.whyWrong: The two axes are orthogonal: PTQ/QAT concerns training-time involvement; dynamic/static concerns scale-computation timing.

misconceptions.claim: Dynamic quantization applies to INT4 and static to INT8; the distinction is by format.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Both apply to any integer format; the distinction is when scales are computed.

misconceptions.claim: Dynamic quantization is always more accurate because it adapts to each input.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Adaptation to a single sample can amplify per-sample outliers; static calibration on a corpus can be more robust.

misconceptions.claim: Static quantization requires QAT; without QAT it cannot be used.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Static PTQ is the most common combination — freeze scales offline without any training-time modification.

implementationFacts: PyTorch `torch.ao.quantization.quantize_dynamic` implements dynamic quantization of Linear/RNN modules.
TensorRT static INT8 uses a calibration cache and IEntropyCalibrator/IEntropyCalibrator2 APIs.
performanceScenarios: For CPU inference of a Transformer, dynamic INT8 quantization saves ~40% latency vs FP32 with minimal accuracy loss.
